title: The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover
dek: Jean Paul Gaultier's costumes change colour when the characters change rooms. It is the most complete integration of clothing into film grammar anyone has managed, in a film whose contempt eventually includes you.

body.text: The device is stated in the first ten minutes and never explained, which is why it works.

Albert Spica's restaurant is colour-zoned: the dining room is red, the kitchen is green, the lavatories are white, the car park outside is blue. Sacha Vierny lights each space to saturation. And as the characters cross between them, their clothes change colour to match. Georgina's corset is scarlet at the table, turquoise in the kitchen, ivory in the bathroom. Outside, in the car park, the Spicas wear black.
Nobody remarks on it. No character notices. There is no in-world justification and the film offers none.
This is the single best costume idea in cinema, and thirty-seven years later almost nothing has come near it.
Why the device is not a gimmick

What Gaultier and Greenaway are doing is dissolving the boundary between costume and production design — and by extension between character and setting. A gimmick would be a joke you notice once. This is a rule the film obeys with total consistency, and consistency turns it into grammar.

Watch what it means. If your clothes are determined by the room you are standing in, you have no self that persists across space. You are an effect of your environment. Albert can dominate every room he enters because he is the room; Georgina's attempts at privacy are undermined by the fact that the building repaints her the moment she moves. When she and Michael conduct their affair in the kitchen, they are wearing the kitchen. There is nowhere to go where you are not wearing where you are.

Greenaway has described the film in terms of a medieval sensibility — a rotting, worm-infested body covered in an extraordinary gloss of elaborate clothing. That is exactly right about the design. Gaultier's contributions are pure surface applied over decay: corsetry that blends Victorian restriction with satin-and-leather seduction, black plumage recurring across Georgina's wardrobe as fascinator and collar and robe, and waiters in crimson military-futurist uniforms with vast lapels and epaulettes that make the staff indistinguishable from the walls.

The register is deliberately unplaceable — Victoriana, Japonisme, militarism, futurism — so that the film can be a satire of 1980s excess without being set in the 1980s. Greenaway's Britain is a timeless one, which makes the argument about greed harder to date and harder to dismiss.
The performances

Michael Gambon is monumentally, exhaustingly good as Albert. It is a performance with no modulation and no interior, and that is the correct choice: Albert has no interior, only volume. Gambon plays him as a man who has never in his life stopped talking long enough to be alone with himself, and the effect after two hours is genuinely oppressive.

Helen Mirren is doing something more difficult with much less material. Georgina is written thin — she is a position in a structure more than a person, defined by what is done to her and by her single act of revenge. Mirren fills that space with a watchfulness that the script does not supply, and the film's emotional weight rests entirely on her willingness to hold still and let the camera find her.

Richard Bohringer's cook is the film's only decent character and correspondingly its least interesting. Alan Howard's lover barely speaks, which is a joke about what Georgina actually wants — someone quiet.
Michael Nyman's score is among the great film scores, a funeral march that keeps arriving too early.
Where I part from the film's admirers
This is a masterpiece and it is also, in a way its fans tend to skate over, deeply misanthropic — and the misanthropy is not confined to its villain.

Greenaway's disgust is total and it is directed at appetite as such: eating, sex, consumption, the body. The film is structured across nine days of menus, and the equation it repeatedly draws between food, sex and violence is not an argument so much as a revulsion. That gives it enormous force and it also flattens it. There is no character in this film who is permitted to want something without being punished for wanting.

The consequence is Georgina. She is the most sympathetic figure and she is also an instrument — her body is the site where Albert's brutality is displayed and the final revenge is executed, and she is given very little that is hers alone. The famous ending is magnificent as a formal gesture and slightly hollow as a character's decision, because Greenaway is more interested in completing the metaphor than in what she would actually do.
I still give it five stars, because the failures are inseparable from the achievement. A less contemptuous film would not have had the nerve to build the colour rule and follow it to the end.
The rating explained

Roger Ebert gave it four stars and noted that its raw emotion set it apart from Greenaway's usually cerebral work — which is right, and is why this is the Greenaway to start with. The MPAA offered Miramax an X; Miramax released it unrated rather than accept the association, and a butchered 95-minute R-rated cut circulated on VHS alongside the 124-minute film. Watch the long one.

Costume design almost never gets to be the organising principle of a film. Here it is not decoration, not characterisation, not even world-building. It is the rule the world runs on, and the rule is stated only in clothes.
Gaultier never got an Academy Award nomination for it. That is not a scandal so much as a category error: there was no award for what he did.
